subject: owl
pitch: A great horned owl perched on a gnarled branch. Mottled bark-brown and buff feathers with fine dark barring, a pale bib at the throat, tall feathered ear tufts, a round tawny facial disc rimmed in black, huge orange eyes and a hooked grey beak. Feathered legs end in strong black talons gripping the wood.
reasoning:
I'm planning a single TypeScript module using the SDK, aiming for clean, error-free code of reasonable size. I'm thinking through the real-world scale of a great horned owl perched on a branch, roughly 0.55m tall, with the model's lowest points (including the branch) resting at floor level.

I'm working out the branch geometry so its bottom touches y=0, with the owl's talons gripping the top around y≈0.18-0.19, and sketching the skeleton hierarchy from hip root through spine, neck, head, legs, and wings using limb and sweep constructs to keep the build manageable while still looking anatomically convincing.

For the body itself, I'm deciding to use scaled sphere primitives to form the plump oval owl shape, relying on the documented scale option for parts rather than a custom loft, and starting to define the hip and chest joints along the spine chain.

Continuing with neck and head joints, I'm deciding the head sits large and close to the body with no real neck gap, centered around y≈0.45, and figuring out orientation using aim points so the bone axes stay well-defined. I'm settling on placing most parts using explicit absolute model-space coordinates rather than relying purely on parent-relative local offsets, since that keeps positioning predictable.

Adding wings and ear tufts...

Adding owl's facial disc, rim, and eye placement...

I'm orienting the cone so it aims forward-down to form a hooked beak shape, adding a small hook sphere at the tip, then placing a pale white bib sphere scaled flatter near the chest.

Now I'm working out leg placement: positioning feathered legs at the hips, defining a limb system from root to foot target, and figuring out the branch geometry so the feet and talons land correctly wrapped around its top surface.

Let me set hip and ankle positions with short lengths and a forward knee bend, calling the limb function to get the leg joint points.

Then I'm planning the toe talons as four rods extending from the ankle point—three forward and one back—each with a small claw spike at the tip.

That toe placement seems fine with slight overlap into the branch. Now I'm figuring out how to draw the toes using the rod helper function, which needs explicit endpoint radius and attaches to the bone of its first point — so I need to determine which bone the ankle joint belongs to, likely by referencing the leg chain's tip.

For the toes and claws, I'm working out how to attach rods to the ankle joint and add small spike shapes extending from each toe tip to represent claws, using direction vectors and short lengths.

Now I'm thinking through the wings, attaching them at the chest joint as elongated sphere shapes positioned and scaled to look folded, and considering how to apply a barring paint pattern across them using stripe bands along a chosen axis.

For the body, I'm layering a mottled paint pattern in brown and buff tones, and double-checking that all paint helpers (mottle, stripes, countershade) and builder functions get imported from the single unified module as the instructions specify.

For the branch, I'm sketching it as a gnarled sweep along a catmull-rom path with a bark color, unattached to any bone so it anchors to the nearest joint to its starting point—likely the root.

I realize 0.02 sinking relative to 0.6 total height is actually 3.3%, which is borderline too much, so I need to adjust the branch geometry so its centerline matches its radius exactly, ensuring the bottom touches y=0 without floating or sinking too far.

I think the cleanest fix is just to let the lowest point of the whole branch touch the ground, so I'll define a dipping centerline with points rising toward both ends and a constant radius, making the middle rest at zero.

I'll add a trunk stub rising from the ground to meet the branch, keeping the lowest points anchored at zero while the branch center sits at 0.12 with radius ~0.11. Then I need to position the owl's feet right on top of the branch surface, adjusting ankle height so the toes rest just above the perch without clipping through it.

Since the branch ends float at x=±0.8 with nothing below, I'll add a stub trunk down to the ground at each end using a short catmull sweep with flat caps so the bottom sits exactly at y=0 instead of dipping below with rounded caps.

I'll settle on stump cylinders radius 0.13 height 0.22 placed at the branch ends, colored dark bark, maybe adding a small knot sphere or side twig for a gnarled look. The branch diameter is a touch thick relative to owl feet proportions, but acceptable for this stylized diorama style.

Since the branch is too chunky for a realistic owl grip, I'm shrinking it to radius 0.05 so the owl's feet sit naturally on top, then working out the leg geometry — hip position, thigh and shank lengths — so the ankles land correctly at the foot contact point on the branch.

I'm overcomplicating the branch radius formula — simplifying to a basic linear taper between two radius values with constant centre height, relying on knots and twigs for the gnarled texture instead. Time to stop refining and just write the final module with carefully chosen joint positions for the ankles and toes.

Now I'm laying out the owl's skeleton hierarchy: hips as root, then chest, neck, and head joints each parented upward with small offsets and aim targets to orient them naturally toward the top of the body.

For the jaw, I'll make the lower beak a part attached to that bone, parented to head without specifying an aim so it just inherits the parent's orientation by default — that simplifies things and avoids extra risk. I'm checking whether joint() actually requires an aim parameter or if it's optional, confirming it's optional.

For the chest I do want an aim so the bone points upward correctly, while neck can just inherit chest's orientation. Now I'm setting up the body geometry using a low-poly sphere with a scale option, defining a helper function for creating spheres, and placing the body part centered on the chest bone.

Then I'm adding a pale belly sphere lower on the front with a barred pattern using alternating buff tones painted via UV stripes, and working out folded wing placement on each side with scaled spheres and a brown/dark striped paint pattern to suggest feathers.

For the head details, I'm placing cone-shaped ear tufts on either side using mirrored positions, carefully positioning them relative to the head sphere's top so they sit naturally at the crown, then defining the head sphere itself slightly offset forward and up from body center.

Now I'm adding the facial disc with a flattened sphere scale in tawny coloring, and a torus ring around it in black to mark the rim of the face. Then I'm placing the eyes as orange spheres with black pupils set forward on the face, adjusting their size and depth to make them prominent like a real owl's.

For the beak, I'm shaping a grey cone angled downward from the head to form the hooked upper beak, with a tiny sphere at the tip to suggest the hook, plus a smaller cone for the lower jaw positioned at the jaw joint.

Then I'm adding a pale bib sphere at the chest just below the head to blend head and body, and setting up the legs by defining hip and ankle points and running them through a limb-bending function with one knee-like joint.

Next I'm chaining each leg with named hip, knee, and ankle bones per side, then sweeping the leg chain with a tapered radius profile to give the legs a feathered look.

Adding toe positions...

Adjusting toe offset so the tip touches the branch surface at 0.10 instead of floating above it, then adding claw spikes at each toe tip with a short length and small radius in black.

Simplifying toes into thicker black rods instead of separate claw spikes, then building the gnarled branch with a catmull sweep, bark coloring and mottled texture, plus small knot bumps and a twig stub sweep...

Writing sweep code...

The branch ends floating in air bothers me, so I'll add small stone pillars at each end to support it—cylinders tapering slightly, bottom resting on the ground and top passing through the branch's centerline. That gives a nice grounded look, like the branch is propped on two rock stumps.

Now I'm checking proportions: the owl's body sphere sits with its bottom just above the legs, hips joint intersecting it correctly. For finishing touches I'm adding a small fanned tail sphere behind the hips, scaled flat, positioned so its bottom clears the branch with a bit of room to spare.

I'm sorting out the surface treatments — mottled brown-and-buff patterns for the body and head, a striped pattern along the "y" axis for wing barring, and a flat tawny tone for the facial disc, making sure each accepts the right color/paint argument type. Then I confirm the builder setup returns the root node correctly, with the tail and all other parts properly parented under the hips joint, keeping geometry counts modest for performance.

I'm working through the joint hierarchy — jaw attaches to the head without its own aim direction so it inherits orientation, while head, neck, and chest joints chain together with aim vectors pointing progressively upward, leaving a small hidden neck segment between stages. I decide the facial disc, eyes, bib, and ear tufts should give enough visual richness without needing scatter/rng utilities, and I skip unused imports to avoid lint errors. Writing imports and body shading code...

Still building the joint hierarchy...

Writing branch sweep code...

Adding small knot details to the stump surface with tiny bark-colored spheres positioned near the top edge.

For the owl body, I'm planning to reuse a single unit sphere geometry across multiple parts, scaling each mesh individually rather than creating separate geometries, which should be efficient as long as sharing doesn't cause unwanted side effects.

Adding wing spheres...

Finishing the tail shape, then moving to the head: adding a mottled ball for the head, a tawny facial disc, and a black torus rim around it for the owl's face.

Adding ear tufts as angled cones with dark brown coloring, and placing orange sphere eyes that slightly protrude on the facial disc.

Now placing the pupil sphere just inside the eye surface so it peeks out as a small black dot, sizing it a bit bigger owl-style. Checking the geometry: at x=±0.036 the head sphere's surface sits around z=0.1085, which lines up well with the eye position at z=0.112.

Now working out the beak: an upper cone angled down-forward from the head, with a small hook sphere placed at its tip, then a separate cone for the lower jaw mandible attached to the jaw bone, and starting to place a pale belly/bib sphere on the chest.

For the legs, I'm computing symmetric hip and ankle positions for left and right, generating limb path points between them, then building each as a chain with named joints (hip, knee, ankle) attached to the hips bone — noting that giving one extra name creates a tip joint beyond the last span.

Then I'm getting the tip joint off each leg (falling back to the last joint if null), sweeping a tapered leg mesh from hip to ankle radius, and finally defining toe offset positions relative to the ankle to generate rod shapes for each toe.

Adding claw spikes...

I'm checking the hip joint position for the leg root attaching correctly into the chain, then verifying the tail ball attaches to the hips joint with the right offset and scale.

Checking that materials, color options, and the builder's part/stripes/mottle/countershade function signatures all match the spec correctly, then finalizing the typed code with proper numeric parameters.

I'll skip adding extra decorative feather details to keep things concise, and wrap up with a short explanation plus the final code block.
